fail.log: You go down on your knees at some point, and you do not recall when. The eye closes. "No," it says, with no feeling at all. You have ten years to think about that word.

choices.text: Look back

effects.log: You look back. It is the stupidest thing you have ever done. Nothing happens for some time. Then something moves in that face, that might have been a smile, when it was alive. You find yourself at the flood stones with white in your hair.

events.text: The head of {bh_the} is down. It is over, and you are sitting in the chair, and the elders are on their knees, and it has all gone better than you had dared to hope. Then every lamp in the hall leans over in the same direction. The oldest elder of all is smiling at the floor. Behind the back hall, a door that you did not know about has opened. "Oh," the old elder says, quite gently. "Did nobody tell you about {bh_anc}?"

choices.text: Stand up, and go out to meet them

effects.log: You go out through the back of the hall, into a cold wind that was not blowing a moment ago. You are shown no great respect, but you are looked at. You have one duel left in you, and you had better make it a good one. (Career: answer the back mountain.)

choices.text: Get down from the chair, and kneel

effects.log: You get down from the chair. It takes more out of you than the head of the house did. A very old person looks at you for a while, and tells you to leave, and you leave, alive. You did not know how much of a mercy that was until you had gone a long way.

events.text: They cheered, some of them. You will remember that. You have been the head of {bh_the} for almost an hour. A servant comes running to tell you that the rice bowl has come back down from the back mountain, on its own, on the step. It is empty. It has never been empty before. The whole hall has stopped talking. Then you hear footsteps on the gravel, very slow, unhurried, and an old, old voice asks who has been sitting in that chair.

choices.text: Answer from the chair: "I am"

effects.log: You do not get up. It is the bravest thing that anyone has ever seen you do, and quite possibly the last. {bh_anc} comes in through the back and stands there, with no expression at all. "Outside," they say. (Career: answer the back mountain.)

choices.text: Rise and bow, and offer them the seat

effects.log: "I do not want it," they say. "Neither do you, I think, not this much. Get out of my grandchildren's house." You get out. In all the years since, you have never told anyone how quickly.

events.text: You knew. You had the name, and you came anyway. So when the wind turns on the back mountain of {bh_the} an hour after the head of the house goes down, you are already standing in the rear yard with your sleeves tied back. {bh_anc} comes down the flood path as if it were a long and tedious errand. "So you are the one who has been asking about me," they say. "You might have come up and asked me to my face."

choices.text: Bow, and tell them you are ready

effects.log: You bow, and you mean it. It is the last time today that anything will be simple. (Career: answer the back mountain.)

choices.text: Say that you were afraid to

effects.log: "Yes," says {bh_anc}, with a sort of sad approval. "That was the first sensible thing anyone has said here all day. Leave the chair, and go, and I will be asleep before you reach the river." You go. It is the sensible thing.

events.text: The head of {bh_the} is on the floor and you are in the chair, and the elders have started to look at the back of the hall, one by one, with a terrible hope. There is the slow sound of someone on the gravel. {bh_anc} comes in, in very old clothes, carrying a rice bowl. They look at the elders. They look at you. They set the bowl down on the arm of your chair. "Keep it filled," they say. And they turn round and walk back up the mountain.

choices.text: Have it filled

effects.log: You have it filled yourself, by your own hand, and you carry it to the flood stones. No one in that hall will ever dare say a word about the blood to your face after that. They will say it behind your back, of course, with their voices low.

choices.text: Watch them go, and say nothing

effects.log: Everyone in the hall watches them go. When you look round the elders are looking at you, and it is not love, but it is at last the correct kind of fear.

events.text: {bh_anc} is sitting on the steps of the back hall of {bh_the}, breathing with some effort, the first time in four hundred years anyone has seen it. They look a good deal smaller than they did. "Well," they say. "I had wondered what that was like." The entire family is standing on the far side of the yard, and nobody is making any sound at all. The chair is yours now, in every way that counts, if you can stand what you do next.

choices.text: Send them back up the mountain, with the rice

effects.log: You help them up, in front of everyone. It takes a while. The family stares. Someone in this house will sing about that for the next hundred years, and they will sing it wrong, and you do not mind that.

choices.text: End it, here on the steps

effects.log: It is very quick. They do not resist, and at the end there is a look of great interest on the old face. No one in that yard makes a sound. There will never again be anything on the back mountain, or anything between you and what this family feels about you.

events.text: The morning after. You are in the chair of {bh_the}, and {bh_oldhead} is alive, somewhere behind a door, because you have not yet said otherwise. Nobody has brought you breakfast, or perhaps that is the custom. The back mountain was silent. Your allies are being very attentive. The whole of the family is waiting to see what sort of person has happened to it.

choices.text: Let {bh_oldhead} go free, with honour

effects.log: You open the door yourself. {bh_oldhead} walks out past you into the morning, without speaking, and all of the family sees it. You have made a dangerous enemy of someone who is still alive. It is the only thing you have done so far that they will not be able to hold against you.

choices.text: Keep them under guard, in comfort

effects.log: A very comfortable room, with a good view. Everyone knows the guards are yours. It is a sensible and a reasonable thing to do, and it is the way these things are generally done, and nobody will ever thank you for it.

choices.text: Exile the whole of that line

effects.log: They leave at noon on carts. There are small children in the carts. Half of the house line up to watch them go, and you hear nobody crying, and that frightens you more than if you had.

events.text: The morning after. You are the head of {bh_the}. {bh_oldhead} is alive, and is sitting in an unheated room, because the sect's law says that it must be so until you decide. Below your window the disciples are drilling in straight lines, the same as yesterday. It is very strange. You had thought it would look different from up here. Everyone has stopped meeting your eye at exactly the same moment.

choices.text: Give {bh_oldhead} back a teaching hall

effects.log: You send them back to teach. It is against every custom there is. The young come to their classes in great numbers, and you can read the mood of the whole sect from how many.

choices.text: Send them down the mountain

effects.log: They go down the mountain with a single bag. They do not look back. A good third of the sect finds some reason to be standing at the gate. You make a note of who.

events.text: The morning after. You are the master of {bh_the}. They have already brought you a very beautiful robe, and the first of the sealed petitions, and a dish to be tasted. There is a tradition concerning what is done with {bh_oldhead}, and everyone is waiting with interest. Strength is law. It is a very simple law, and it means that from this morning on, every one of them is now doing arithmetic about you.

choices.text: Do what is traditional

effects.log: You do it on the terrace, with the whole Cult watching. Everyone nods, and the arithmetic slows down for a while. It is the first order you have given here, and it is the one they understood.

choices.text: Keep {bh_oldhead} alive, and useful

effects.log: You send {bh_oldhead} to the southern mines, under your own seal. In the Cult that is either the most frightening thing you could have done or the most foolish. They will test which. They are probably starting now.

events.text: You wake in a charcoal burner's hut, a long way from the walls you were thrown out of. Somebody has set your left arm, very badly. Your name has been struck from every roll in the province, the burner's wife says cheerfully, and there is a reward, but not much of one, and she wants to know if you take your rice with salt. Everything you built in that house was built on a chair you could not reach. Your arms still work. Mostly.

choices.text: Eat the rice, and start over

effects.log: You eat the rice. It has salt in it. It is the best thing you have ever tasted. There are people in that house who will sleep very badly the day they hear that you lived.

choices.text: Leave at once, before the reward gets bigger

effects.log: You leave a coin on the step and you go on foot into the hills, and you do not stop for a long time. You are getting quite good at that.

events.text: You will not get those years back. You sit on the bank of the river at the edge of the family's lands, with a wound that aches and a name that is now a kind of joke in the teahouses: "as loyal as a guest of the great houses." From here you can still see the roof of the upper hall. You can also see that one lamp in the guest wing has been lit, very faintly, as it was every night that you lived there. Someone has put it there on purpose.

choices.text: Bow toward the lamp, and go

effects.log: You do not know who it was. You bow anyway, and you walk away with your back very straight, in case anyone is looking, and in case nobody is.

choices.text: Swear they will see you again

effects.log: You say it aloud, once, to the river. It is not a very sensible oath. Your heart feels a good deal better for having said it, and a good deal worse.

events.text: You took the seat of {bh_the} by force, and {npc} is here to remind you that this has consequences. The ancestral rites are to be held, and it turns out that no one can be found who is willing to read the names, if it is you standing there. The priests are sick, all of them. So is the cantor. {npc} is sorry to hear it, and {he} has never looked better.

choices.text: Read them yourself, without a priest

effects.log: You read all nine hundred years in your own voice. Your pronunciation is not good. Half of the family walks out at the first name, and the other half stay until the end. You know exactly who stayed now.

choices.text: Cancel the rites

effects.log: The rites are cancelled, for the first time since the fall of the old dynasty. It is a good deal cheaper than you expected. It costs you everything that it was always going to cost you.

choices.text: Pay the priests' families a visit, and see who is making them sick

ok.log: The cantor is up by the second day, and singing, a little off key. It was never about the priests, and now {npc} knows that you know that.

fail.log: They are very polite, and they are very sick, and you drink a lot of tea with people who are just waiting for you to leave.

events.text: There is a child's drawing nailed to the door of the head's room of {bh_the}. It shows a figure in a chair with its head coming off, and it has been done with great attention to the neck. You know the child: eight years old, a grandchild of {bh_oldhead}. You have also seen {npc} teaching the small hand to hold a brush. The child is watching you read it from the far end of the corridor, and is not afraid.

choices.text: Go and get down on one knee, and ask what the seat should do

effects.log: The child looks at you for a long time, and then tells you about the fish in the east pond. You have them restocked. It is the first time in years that anyone in this family has seen you do anything for no reason.

choices.text: Take down the drawing, and keep it

effects.log: It goes in the drawer of your desk. There will be others over the years, and the necks do get better. You keep all of them. Someone ought to.

events.text: You have just learned why your soup has been so good. You have a new cook. The old cook of {bh_the} walked out on the morning of your victory, along with all the people who knew how the drains work, where the river keys are, and how to read the old grain books. They are at an inn in the town, and they have been very well paid by {npc}. Today, your hall has been flooded, for the second time this month, and the rice is wet.

choices.text: Go to the inn in person, and ask the old cook what it would take

ok.log: The old cook wants an apology, and not from you: you are to make {npc} say that the old head's tea was never properly hot. It takes a certain amount of doing. The drains are working by the end of the month.

fail.log: The old cook gives you a very good lunch, and tells you nothing, and there is a bill.

choices.text: Hire new people, whatever it costs

effects.log: They do not know the old drains, and they will never be told. It takes three years, and your whole treasury is damp. But in the end the house runs on people who answer to you, and they have no idea what they missed.

events.text: A whole branch of the family has written to you, in very fine language, to say that it will be holding its own New Year rites, under its own elder, in its own hall, and that it wishes you long life. That is about a third of the fighting strength of {bh_the}. {npc} carried the letter here in person. {He} would very much like to watch your face while you read it.

choices.text: Ride out there, alone, and sit down at their table

effects.log: You sit down at their New Year table unasked, and you eat what is put in front of you. Everyone watches you chew. By the end of the night no one has the nerve to throw you out, and in the morning the letter is withdrawn. It is all said to be a misunderstanding.

choices.text: Let them go, and hold what you have

effects.log: You let them go. The house is smaller, and so is the size of the problem. You can hear {npc} being disappointed from the other side of the compound.

events.text: The eldest of the great-aunts of {bh_the}, one hundred and three, has asked to be carried into the main hall, after twenty years away from it. The chair is set down in front of you, in front of the whole family, and the look takes a long time. "I knew your kind," comes at last, clear as a bell. "We ate one, about four hundred years ago. It took three generations." {npc} is looking at the floor, very pleased about something.

choices.text: Ask how it was done

effects.log: There is a silence. Then the old one begins to laugh, without any sound, the whole small body shaking. "Oh, that one would have liked you. Bring your chair over here." You sit, and you are told. It is the most frightening afternoon of your life, and it may be the most useful.

choices.text: Bow, and have the old one carried home with honour

effects.log: You bow very low, because it has been earned. The chair is carried out with every honour you can think of. It is the correct thing to do, and everyone saw that you did it, and nobody thanks you.

events.text: The disciples of {bh_the} still bow to you. They have started doing it very exactly, to the proper depth, and then counting to the proper number. {npc} has been teaching them this. It is the most insulting thing you have ever seen. There is nothing in the sect's rule you could punish it under. You could not have written a better rule, and you know because you have been looking.

choices.text: Start bowing back, exactly as deep, to all of them

effects.log: You do it for a year. You bow to the kitchen boys. They do not know what to do. In the end some of them start bowing properly, out of pure embarrassment.

choices.text: Make {npc} the master of etiquette

effects.log: It is an extremely dull post, and it comes with a great many forms. {npc} bows to you exactly the proper depth when you hand {him} the seal. You think there is some respect in it, and you are almost sure.

mem.note: gave me a post made of forms

events.text: Half of the good teachers of {bh_the} have asked leave to go on pilgrimage, all in the same month. {npc} has drawn up the list and presents it, with sympathy, for your seal. The young will have no one to teach them but you. {bh_oldhead} is said to be living in a small temple a few days' walk away, and it is said that the road there has become very busy.

choices.text: Go there yourself, and ask them to come back

effects.log: You walk there. {bh_oldhead} gives you some weak tea and a long look. "No," they say, "but I will tell them to teach." They do. It takes you some time to work out how you feel about being helped.

choices.text: Teach the classes yourself

effects.log: You teach eleven classes a day for two years, and you are quite bad at it at first. Your cultivation suffers. The young ones turn out better than you had any right to expect, and they are yours now.

events.text: In {bh_the} strength is law. That law now says that everyone who wants what you have has only to be stronger than you on one single evening. Tonight, it is {npc}, who was very loyal to {bh_oldhead} and who has been very patient. {He} has come into your rooms with no weapon, and has sat down, and has asked you what you think of the wine. There is something wrong with the air in here.

choices.text: Set down the cup, and ask {him} what {he} thinks of your chances

ok.log: It ends in the middle of a sentence. {npc} is carried out, and the hall knows by morning, and for some time after that the arithmetic in the upper halls comes out in your favour.

fail.log: It is very close. You are on the floor for a while, and so is {he}, and {he} gets up first and leaves. Everyone will know by morning that {he} could have stayed.

choices.text: Open the window, and offer {him} a command

effects.log: The air clears. It was never about the wine. {npc} takes the command, and looks at you with new respect and with a precise idea of what you are afraid of.

events.text: The great bronze bell of {bh_the} has been rung for a change of master every time in its history, and it has not rung for you. {npc} has the only key to the bell tower. {He} regrets very much that it has been lost, and is having a new one cut, and that it will take a while. The whole mountain is listening to that silence each morning. It is getting to be a kind of opinion.

choices.text: Have the tower door cut down, and ring it yourself

effects.log: You ring it yourself, badly, with the whole Cult standing in the yard. It is ridiculous and it is effective. You have ringing hands for a week. Nobody laughs, or not where you can hear it.

choices.text: Have the bell melted down, and made into something useful

effects.log: There is a great deal of bronze in it. You make it into very good arrowheads. It is the most terrible thing you could possibly have done, and it took you one morning, and the whole of the Cult respects you for it.

events.text: A delegation of the old families of {bh_the} has come to see you, quite formally, with its hands empty. They would like to discuss what it would cost. They are not forgiving anything, and they are at pains to say so. There is a matter of old debts, and of restoring a certain line to its place, and it would have to be done in public, on your knees, before the tablets. It would be expensive, in many ways. It would also end some of this.

choices.text: Pay it, in full, and kneel

effects.log: You kneel. It is a long ceremony and the stone is cold. There are several people who have waited a long time to see this, and they enjoy it very much. It costs you a fortune and a good deal else, and it buys something that nothing else could have.

choices.text: Offer them something smaller

effects.log: They listen, and they consider, and they thank you. Then they go home. It was a good offer, and it was not what they came for. Nobody tries to poison you for several months.

choices.text: Send them away

effects.log: You send them away. It is your right, and you hold the seat. They leave very quietly, and you find out in time how much of the house went with them.

events.text: Your eldest ally in {bh_the} comes to you late at night, and gives you some advice you did not ask for. "Nobody will ever love you for it," they say. "But the old head had a son, and that son has a boy who shows promise. Name that boy your heir before the tablets. It costs you everything you did it for. In return, your grandchildren get to live here." They wait. They are very tired. Below you in the dark somebody is singing the old family song.

choices.text: Name the boy, and take what comes

effects.log: You say it before the tablets, in a voice you would not have recognized a year ago. It does not make them love you. But the song stops being sung outside your window, and starts being sung somewhere further off.

choices.text: Say that your blood will sit here, or nobody's will

effects.log: You say it. Your ally nods very slowly, and bows, and goes to bed. In the morning they have left you a small gift and a letter of resignation.

events.text: It has been a long time. A very old elder of {bh_the}, who has refused to speak to you for all of it, has fallen ill. You find out from the laundry that there is a very expensive medicine that the family can no longer afford, and that everyone has been told not to mention this to you. You know the old fool has been planning your death for a decade. You also know that you have the medicine.

choices.text: Send it, with no name on it

effects.log: It arrives. The old fool recovers. No one says anything at all. Some months later, for the first time in your whole reign, somebody stands when you walk into the hall. It is that old elder, and it takes an extremely long time.

choices.text: Let it take its course

effects.log: It takes its course. There is a very large funeral, and you preside. Everyone is careful to remark on how moved you looked. You are, a little. It is one fewer.

events.text: You have asked. In {bh_the} nobody has ever just asked. {bh_head} sits with the register open at a clean page, and the elders are on either side, and they have all read every word that was ever written about you. It takes them most of a day to recite your deeds. It is a very long list. It is also clear from their faces that this is what they are holding against you. "Why," says {bh_head}, finally, "should this house take in someone who does not need it?"

choices.text: "Because it is going to need me, and you know it"

ok.log: It is not the correct answer, and there is a silence. But the pen moves. Your name goes down in a very small hand at the bottom of the page. Half the elders do not look up. You are of the house now, and in your life you will never have to ask for anything so hard again.

fail.log: {bh_head} closes the register very gently. "Quite," they say. They do not ask you to leave the house. They will never ask you this again, and you will never ask them.

choices.text: "Because I have nowhere else I want to die"

ok.log: Nobody says anything for some time. An old woman at the end of the table has started to cry, and is furious about it. The pen moves. It is the truest thing you have ever said in this house, and you are never going to know whether you meant it.

fail.log: It is a beautiful line. They have heard beautiful lines before. The register closes.

choices.text: Say you have changed your mind, and leave

effects.log: You stand and you bow. They look a little disappointed, for some reason. The clean page stays clean. The house stays what it was to you, for now.

events.text: The whole of the family has been called to witness. {bh_the} has not adopted anyone from outside in two hundred years, and there is no real ceremony for it, so they have had to look one up. You are to kneel on the bare stone and be asked three times whether you give up your own ancestors. The priest is sweating. {bh_heir} is watching with no expression at all. You have been thinking about your own mother a good deal this morning.

choices.text: Answer yes, three times

effects.log: Three times you say it, in a clear voice. You feel nothing the first time. You feel it a little the second. They write you down, and everyone bows, and many of them hate you more than ever. Your own tablets are somewhere very far away, and they have gone quiet.

choices.text: Answer: "I keep them, and I take on yours as well"

ok.log: There is an appalling silence. Then a very old man of the blood barks a laugh and says that this is what the first ancestor said, and it is true, it is in the book, and now no one can object. The pen moves, and you have your name, and you kept theirs.

fail.log: The priest loses his place, and the old men get to their feet. It takes a long time for the shouting to stop. There will not be a second ceremony.

events.text: It has happened very quickly. {bh_head} is dying in the inner room of a thing the physicians have stopped giving a name to. The heir has been dead a month. There is a child, seven or eight, who has been told to stop crying, and there are a great many cousins out in the corridor counting on their fingers. {bh_head} has sent for you, of all people, and is holding your wrist with a surprisingly strong hand. "They will tear each other to pieces. You are the only one who has no blood to want it for. Hold the seal for the child. Swear."

choices.text: Swear, and take the seal

effects.log: You swear it. The hand on your wrist lets go. In the corridor they stop counting when you come out with the seal in your hand, and you can actually hear them start again. You are the most powerful person in this house now, and you are not its head, and a small child is looking up at you.

choices.text: Refuse, and let the cousins have it

effects.log: You take the hand from your wrist, very gently, and you say no. {bh_head} looks at you for a long moment, and does not ask again. The fighting goes on through the winter. You have kept your hands clean, and you will always know that you did it on purpose.

events.text: The elders of {bh_the} have come to you in a body, in the middle of the night, and they look extremely unhappy about it. {bh_head} has only days left. The only child of the line is too small to hold a spoon properly, let alone the seal, and the branches have each brought their swords to the funeral. None of them can stand to see any of the others do it. "You are outside the blood," the eldest says, as if it hurt. "It can be undone, at the child's coming of age. It must be undone. We need your word."

choices.text: Give your word

effects.log: They hate this. It is quite marvellous to see how much. They bow to you one by one, and they put the seal into your hands. Over their heads, a nursemaid is trying to get a small person to put down a dead beetle.

choices.text: Decline: you are not the one for it

effects.log: They are relieved, and horrified. The branches go to war over the funeral meats. You stand well back. Quite a few people will remember you stood back, and they will not all mean it kindly.

events.text: {bh_child}, head of {bh_the}, is sitting in the great chair with both feet off the floor and has asked you, in front of the whole audience, why the river envoy has such a big nose. It does not get any easier. You have been ruling this family in that voice for years now. You have got rather good at saying "The head of the house thanks you" while you are holding a very small sticky hand behind the arm of the chair.

choices.text: Teach {bh_child} how to read a room

effects.log: You teach it, in the evenings, with the envoys' letters. It is a very sharp small head. You had not planned on enjoying this, or on how quickly you are starting to be seen through.

choices.text: Keep the lessons to rites and calligraphy

effects.log: The child learns a beautiful hand, and all the proper bows. Nobody could possibly object. It is an extremely quiet way of making sure that nobody will ever need to be asked to give you anything back.

events.text: A cousin of the blood has come to you with an excellent idea. {bh_child} is delicate, as everyone knows, and the winters here are hard. It would be so much better for the child to go south, for some years, for their health, and it would be a great relief to everyone if there were someone suitable to look after things here for even longer. This cousin has brought a physician who agrees, and is not asking you to do anything: only not to do anything.

choices.text: Have the cousin thrown down the steps

effects.log: Quite literally. The physician leaves on his own. {bh_child} hears about it, as they hear about everything, and that night a very small person brings you a very badly made cup of tea.

choices.text: Say you will consider it, and let the cousin go

effects.log: You say you will consider it. You do. You consider it for a whole evening, and you have the window open so that you can hear someone small being told to go to bed. Then you burn the physician's letter. You are not quite sure which of you that was for.

events.text: The Governor has sent an inspector, who has asked politely to whom, exactly, {bh_the} now answers: the child, or the person who holds the child's seal? He would so like it clarified. The elders have turned out to watch. {bh_child} is sitting up very straight in the chair, and has clearly been coached by someone, and it was not you. They look at you, and then at the inspector, and open their mouth.

choices.text: Say nothing, and let the child answer

effects.log: "To me," says a small clear voice. "That one holds it for me." The hall lets out its breath. You keep your face perfectly still. You have never been prouder, and you have never been so clearly told how long you have left.

choices.text: Answer first, and smoothly

effects.log: You answer before the small mouth can make a sound. It is a good answer. The inspector is satisfied. {bh_child} closes their mouth, and does not look at you again that day.

events.text: {bh_child} is sixteen today. They have come to your rooms in their good robes, and they are alone, and they are taller than you remember. They do not ask you for it. They sit down in the chair for visitors and they look at the seal on your desk. They have your way of sitting, you notice, and there is no one else in this house who could have taught them that. "It is the day," they say. "I would like to know what you are going to do."

choices.text: Put it in their hands

effects.log: You walk it across the room, and it is the shortest and the longest walk in the world. They weigh it, and they nod. Then they bow to you, deeply, in the old way, and they are the only one of the blood who ever has. Your power is gone by the evening. You sleep better than you have slept in a decade.

choices.text: Say the house is not ready, and ask for a few years more

effects.log: They look at you. They have your way of looking. "No," they say, quite calmly, "but I expect you will take them." They go out. It is not a threat. You know, because you taught them how to make one.

choices.text: Tell them the seal is yours now

effects.log: You say it. It is very quiet. They do not look surprised. That is what hurts, you find, more than you had planned. By morning you are the head of {bh_the} in name as well, and you will have to find something to do with a sixteen-year-old who knows you better than anyone alive.

events.text: You have held the seal of {bh_the} for a long time, and the day you swore to has come, and it is raining. {bh_child} has grown into someone careful. The elders have arranged themselves around the courtyard with a good view. Half of them are hoping you will keep it, because then they can finally destroy you, and the other half are hoping you will give it up, because then they can finally destroy you. There is an empty place at the table in front of the tablets.

choices.text: Lay the seal on the table, in the rain, and step back

effects.log: You lay it down and you step back. {bh_child} picks it up. Somebody in the crowd has started to cry, and you think it is the eldest elder, who hates you. The rain runs into your collar. It is the best thing that you have ever done, and hardly anybody will say so.

choices.text: Walk to the table, and sit down in the empty place

effects.log: You sit, and you put the seal down in front of you and you fold your hands on it. Nobody breathes. You have ruled here for years in all but name, and now you have only said so out loud. The rain goes on. So will the hatred.

events.text: There is an outsider at the lower table of {bh_the}, one of the guest retainers, and your cousin {npc} has been told to keep an eye on them, and has asked you to help. They are good, you have to admit. They are much too good. They took the east road bandits apart last spring and did not even ask for a bonus. "It is just that nobody knows what they want," {npc} says. "It would be such a shame if someone were to find out they wanted something."

choices.text: Help keep watch, as family

effects.log: You keep watch. It is very dull. They eat, they train, they bow to you a little late. You make your report. It is only when you are going to sleep that you think how carefully you have just described someone's whole life.

choices.text: Go and speak to the outsider yourself

effects.log: You go and you sit at the lower table, which nobody of the name has done in years. They are very polite. You can feel the whole upper table watching you be friendly. You find out they are funny. {npc} would like a word.

events.text: At dinner the talk has turned to the guest who saved the salt road. {npc} is doing the voice. Everyone laughs, the voice is very good. You rode with that guest on the salt road. You were twenty and you were going to die, and they went back for you, with a wound, and never mentioned it after. You are sitting with your own people. Your bowl is getting cold.

choices.text: Laugh with the others

effects.log: You laugh with the others. It is easy. It is so very easy. You pass that guest in the yard next morning. They nod to you exactly as they always do, and you wish very much that they would not.

choices.text: Say what happened on the salt road

ok.log: The table goes a bit quiet. "Of course they did," {npc} says after a moment, not doing the voice. It does not change anything much. But someone at the lower table has heard, and you find a jar of good pickles outside your door.

fail.log: You say it, and {npc} looks at you with a kind of pity. "They are very good at that, you know. Getting you to think it was your idea." Nobody mentions it again.

events.text: You were born to all this. You have never once in your life had to ask where you would sit. It occurs to you, in your thirtieth or fortieth year in {bh_the}, watching {npc} go through the old ceremony of telling a guest retainer that they are not to touch the tablets, that this person has lived here longer than you have. They are carrying the bucket. They have never spilled any. It is an odd thing to notice.

choices.text: Take the other handle of the bucket

effects.log: It is heavier than it looks. They look at you sideways, and they do not say anything, and you carry it the whole way together. {npc} has several things to say to you about it afterward, and you find you do not care for any of them.

choices.text: Go on to the rites

effects.log: You go on to the rites. Your name is the one that is read. It has always been a comfort. It is still a comfort, nearly.

events.text: Your place is secure. Your name is on the register. Which makes it interesting that {npc} has come to you to say that a certain rival, of the same blood, has been spending evenings with one of the guest retainers. A strong one. They could not sit in the chair themselves, of course. "But they could certainly put someone in it," says {npc}. "I thought you would want to know, as family."

choices.text: Warn the head of the house

effects.log: You do. You are thanked, and watched, and the rival is sent to the northern estates. The guest retainer is moved to a better room with a better view of nothing. It all goes very smoothly, and you did that.

choices.text: Go and make a better offer to the guest yourself

effects.log: You go. They hear you out with the most courteous expression you have ever seen. You come away with the distinct impression that you are now the third of this family to have tried this.

events.text: The old register of {bh_the} has come to you to be copied, as an honour. Going through it you find a name, four hundred years back, that has been written over, in a different ink. The first of your line to hold the seat. Under the new name, in faint brown, is the name of a guest retainer. You sit looking at it for a long time. {npc} is coming up the stairs.

choices.text: Copy it as it stands, and say nothing

effects.log: You copy it out in your best hand. You will be the only person alive who knows. It gives you an odd feeling at the rites now, and you look at the guests at the lower table a little longer than you used to.

choices.text: Show {npc}

effects.log: {npc} looks at it for a moment, and then looks at you, and very gently closes the book. "Everyone knows that," {he} says. "Don't you know? Why do you think we are so careful?"

events.text: You hold the seat of {bh_the}, by right, by blood, and so it falls to you to carry up the rice. It is one bowl, once a year. No one told you about this until the day you took the chair, and now you know why. {bh_anc} takes it from your hands without looking at you. "You are the what, the nineteenth?" they say. "You all have the same chin. Is anybody trying to kill you yet? No? You are not doing it right."

choices.text: Stay a while, and ask how it was done

effects.log: They tell you, for most of a day, with enormous enjoyment. It is the most honest account of the history of this family you have ever heard, and it is nothing like the one on the tablets. You come down very thoughtful.

choices.text: Bow, set it down, and leave

effects.log: You bow and you go. It is what the one before you did, and the one before that. Behind you someone is eating rice with a very good appetite.

events.text: A hard year for {bh_the}. You have carried up the rice as usual. For the first time in your life, you have stayed on the step and asked for help. There are enemies at the river, and the treasury is thin, and a nephew who thinks you are a fool. {bh_anc} goes on eating for some time. "No," they say. "If it can be finished by anything less than the end of the world, it deserves to be. I only come down for one thing. You know what it is. Is that what is happening?"

choices.text: Say no, and thank them

effects.log: "Good," they say. "Go and sort it out. You have the chin for it." You go down. It is ridiculous how much better you feel. You manage the river and the treasury, and the nephew still thinks you are a fool.

choices.text: Ask them to teach you one thing, only one

ok.log: They look at you, for the first time in all the years you have come here. Then they take your wrist, and they move it about an inch. "There," says {bh_anc}. "This whole family has been doing that wrong since the third generation." You will spend ten years understanding it.

fail.log: They finish the rice and hand you the bowl. "Next year," they say. They have said that to all of you.

events.text: {bh_head} has taken the chair of {bh_the}, and the first thing they do is ask for the guest roll. They go down it with a brush. Everything the last head granted you, they say courteously, was granted by the last head. They would like to get to know you. It is the same sentence you were told when you came here, in nearly the same voice, by someone who was not yet born.

choices.text: Bow, and begin again

effects.log: You bow, and you begin again: the lower step, the careful answers. You have done it before, and you know where the loose boards are. They do not know that yet.

choices.text: Remind them, gently, what the last head was afraid of

ok.log: You say very little. They set down the brush and look at you properly for the first time. Your rooms stay your rooms. Their eyes stay on you.

fail.log: They hear a threat, because it was one. By evening your name has moved to a shorter list.

events.text: The old head of {bh_the} is in the ground, and {bh_head} holds the seal. The funeral meats are still on the table when the new head comes to sit beside you, of all people, with a jug. "You knew the old one better than any of us," they say. "So tell me. What did they promise you, and how much of it do you think I am going to keep?" They are smiling. They have been waiting years to ask.

choices.text: "Nothing you need keep"

effects.log: They laugh and fill your cup. You have given up a good deal, and they know exactly how much. You will find out over the next few years what that buys.

choices.text: Name every promise, and the year it was made

effects.log: You name them all, with dates. They listen to the end, nodding, and write none of it down. You have told them what you want. That may have been the point of the jug.

events.text: You have now outlasted another head of {bh_the}. {bh_head} is the third you have knelt to, or the fifth; the house has stopped counting and you have not. At the installing, the young of the blood look at you with open curiosity, the way one looks at a very old tree that nobody remembers planting. The new head bows to you first, by a hair, and nobody can say whether it was a mistake.

choices.text: Bow back by exactly the same hair

effects.log: You bow by exactly that much. The old aunts draw in their breath. It will be argued over in the family wing for a generation, and you are content to let it.

choices.text: Go down on the stone with everyone else

effects.log: You go down with all the rest, and your knees remember how. The new head looks relieved, and then, a little later, thoughtful.

events.text: {bh_head} now leads {bh_the}. By custom every senior renews their token before the new seat, and by custom this means nothing. But the new head has read your record, all of it, and has put a small slip of paper in it at the page you hoped they would skip. They hand your token back without taking the slip out. "We should talk sometime," they say, and call the next name.

choices.text: Ask for that talk today

effects.log: You go up that evening, and you talk for two hours about nothing. Both of you leave with a very clear idea of the other. It is the most honest conversation you have had on this mountain.

choices.text: Wait to be called

effects.log: You wait. They do not call. The slip stays in your record, and every month you find you are thinking about it.

events.text: The new leader of {bh_the} has moved the seniors' seats. It is a small thing: yours is now two down and one across, beside a window that does not close. Whatever you had arranged with the last leader, you are given to understand, is a matter for the archive. The disciples are watching to see whether you notice. You have been sitting in that hall since before most of them were born.

choices.text: Sit by the window, and bring a shawl

effects.log: You bring a shawl. It is a very old shawl. Within a year the juniors think of that seat as the senior one, and the new leader is looking at the window.

choices.text: Take your old seat, and let them ask you to move

effects.log: You sit where you always sat. Nobody asks you to move. Everybody saw. The leader goes on with the meeting as if nothing had happened, which is how you know you will pay for it.

events.text: The last master of {bh_the} is gone, by the usual road, and {bh_head} is on the high terrace. They have sent you a cup, an empty one, with no message. In the upper halls this is read in three ways, and you have heard them all by noon. The people who used to do your arithmetic are doing it again, from the beginning. You have rather good odds. You have also seen what good odds are worth here.

choices.text: Send the cup back full

effects.log: You fill it with your best wine and send it up. It comes back washed. Nobody has died yet, and in the Cult that counts as a warm beginning.

choices.text: Go up and lift it in front of them

effects.log: You climb the terrace, you pour for yourself, and raise it, and set it down. Nothing happens. The new master applauds, softly. You have shown that you are not afraid, and now they will have to find out if that is true.

events.text: {bh_head} sits the seat of {bh_the} now, and every senior is to bring a gift. Gifts are how the Cult finds out what you have been hiding. Bring too little and you are a fool or an insult. Bring too much and you are a rival who has just told everyone the size of the treasury. There is a long line on the steps, and everyone in it is sweating gently and looking at everyone else's boxes.

choices.text: Bring a list of who has been stealing from the seat

effects.log: It is a short list, and an accurate one, and you are not on it. The new master reads it twice. Several people on the steps behind you will not be needing their boxes.

choices.text: Bring a modest gift, and a very straight back

effects.log: It is a modest gift. Nobody is fooled. You have told them that you can count, and that you are not yet ready to be counted.

events.text: A new retainer at {bh_the} asks you, very kindly, whether you have been here long, and whether you would like help with that bucket. {npc} has told the young ones you are simple, as {his} grandfather told {his} father. It is a family tradition now. You have been insulted here by five generations of the same nose, and you have begun to feel something like affection for the nose.

choices.text: Accept the help, and ask after the grandfather

effects.log: You ask after the grandfather by name, and you repeat what was said to you on the east stairs, a hundred years ago, word for word. {npc} is a good deal quieter at dinner.

choices.text: Carry it yourself

effects.log: You carry it yourself. You have carried it past every one of them. The stairs have a groove in them now, and it is yours, and nobody else in this house has left a mark that deep.

events.text: They are repainting the guest wing of {bh_the}, and {npc} has come to ask if you would mind moving, just for a season, into the old storeroom. You helped build that storeroom. You remember when the whole wing was a stand of pines. {npc} is explaining the history of the house to you, slowly, with some errors, and {he} is very proud of it.

choices.text: Listen to the end, and thank {him}

effects.log: You listen. You learn that your own best deed is now credited to somebody's uncle. It makes you laugh that evening, alone among the old jars, for rather longer than you expected.

choices.text: Correct {him}, with the dates

ok.log: You correct {him}, gently, for an hour. By the end a few of the young have gathered to listen and {npc} has stopped talking. You find a stool outside your door the next day: they want the rest of it.

fail.log: You remember the dates perfectly. {npc} looks at you with real pity, and asks if you have been sleeping.

events.text: The law of {bh_the} says that a guest may not grow old at the family's expense past a certain term. Nobody has ever needed that law before. {npc} has found it and is reading it out, delighted, to the council: a guest of more than a hundred years must be either made kin, sent away, or formally thanked. They have settled on formally thanked. There is to be a small plaque.

choices.text: Attend the unveiling, and admire the plaque

effects.log: It is a very small plaque. It spells your name wrong. You make a graceful speech and keep the seat. A plaque is what a family gives someone it cannot get rid of.

choices.text: Ask them to read the first two options again

effects.log: You ask, politely, which of the other two they would prefer to try. The silence goes on long enough for a sparrow to come in and leave. The plaque goes up very quietly.

events.text: The one you married into {bh_the} has been in the family plot for longer than some of its elders have been alive. {npc} points out, with sympathy, that the marriage is therefore a matter of history, and asks whether you have thought about where you would like to go. You still have the crest. You have also buried three of the people who taught {him} to say things like that.

choices.text: Say you will stay beside your dead

effects.log: You say it. Nobody can argue with it, and {npc} does not try. You go out to the plot in the evening and tell the headstone all about it. It is still the best listener in the family.

choices.text: Ask {him} to name the elder who could make you leave

effects.log: You wait. {npc} goes through the names in {his} head. You watch {him} reach the end of the list.

events.text: You were written into the register of {bh_the} so long ago that the ink of your line has gone the same brown as the founder's. {npc} found you in it last week while looking for something else, and has asked the archivist whether the page might be damp. It is not damp. {He} does not know whether you were born here. Nobody at the table does. You could simply stop mentioning it.

choices.text: Say nothing, and let it be forgotten

effects.log: You say nothing. A child at the rites asks which branch you are from, and an old aunt answers without thinking. So that is how it ends: not with acceptance, but with nobody left who remembers to object.

choices.text: Tell the young, every year, exactly how you came here

effects.log: You tell them at every New Year. It annoys everyone. You did not cross that stone on your knees to be mistaken for someone who never had to.

events.text: You have held the chair of {bh_the} for longer than the house had been a house when you took it. {npc}, who is young, has made a speech at the rites saying that the time has come for the seat to return to the blood. It is a good speech. The old fury in the hall has gone out of it, though: half of the family has your chin by now, through one marriage or another, and they are looking around at each other.

choices.text: Applaud the speech

effects.log: You applaud, and you mean it. It is well built. You offer {him} a post in charge of something difficult and far away, and {he} takes it, and you think {he} may turn out quite well.

choices.text: Ask {him} whose blood {he} means

effects.log: You ask it kindly. {npc} opens {his} mouth. The registers are brought out, and it takes three days, and no one ever makes that speech in your hearing again.

events.text: {npc} has been told, by {his} father, who was told by {his} father, that you are not to be provoked. {He} would like to know why. {He} has come to your rooms to ask you, honestly, with a practice sword and very good manners, and {he} is the first person in this house in a hundred years who has wanted to see for {him}self. You had forgotten what that looks like.

choices.text: Show {him}, as gently as you can

ok.log: {He} wakes on your floor about an hour later, with a blanket over {him}. "Oh," says {npc}. "I see." {He} comes back the next week. You have not had a student you liked this much in a very long time.

mem.note: put a blanket over me afterward

fail.log: It is {npc} who is gentle with you, in the end. You have not been paying attention, these last decades. It is a very useful thing to learn from someone who is still polite.

choices.text: Tell {him} the story, and send {him} away

effects.log: You tell {him}. It takes a long time, and it is mostly about people {he} has only read about on tablets. {He} goes out very quietly.

events.text: Three branches of {bh_the} have come to you this year, separately and by night, each wanting your support against the others. You remember when their founders were three cousins fighting over a mule. {npc} has been the last to come, and {he} is the only one who did not bring a gift. It occurs to you that you have become one of the old powers of this house, as the tablets are, as the back mountain is.

choices.text: Send all three home with the same answer

effects.log: You tell each of them about the mule. Two are offended. The third, {npc}, laughs until {he} has to sit down. The quarrel goes on, but more quietly, and nobody draws a blade at New Year.

choices.text: Back {npc}, and see what you have made

effects.log: You back {him}. It takes about a year, and the house is a different shape afterward. You have not moved anything in a long time, and it turns out you still can.

events.text: You have sat through something like four hundred council days at {bh_the}, always by the door. Today a young elder has asked what the house did the last time the river rose this high. There is a silence, and then every head at the table turns slowly toward you, for it was a hundred and twenty years ago and you are the only one who was there. They have never all looked at you at once before.

choices.text: Tell them what was done, and what it cost

effects.log: You tell them. It takes all afternoon. They do what you say, and it works, and they move your seat one place up from the door, for reasons they leave unstated.

choices.text: Tell them it is in the archive, and let them look

effects.log: It is not in the archive. Someone burned that page, which you also remember. You let them look, and you wait, and when they come back they are a good deal more polite.

events.text: A delegation from {bh_the}, with a very large box. The house has decided to create a new dignity for you, Venerable Pillar, which has no duties at all, comes with a hall on the far lake, and may be held for life, however long that proves to be. It has been noticed that several of the people you have outlived held similar titles, and that it kept them quiet at the end. The youngest of the delegation is trying not to stare at your hands.

choices.text: Accept the Venerable Pillar

effects.log: It is a very nice hall. You spend a few years there, feeding carp. You come back to the main house whenever you like, of course. Nobody thought to write down that you could not.

choices.text: Say you will consider it, as you did the last three

effects.log: You have a shelf for these by now. The delegation bows and leaves the box. In your experience the next one will be bigger, and it will come from someone who is more afraid.

events.text: The stone in the hall of {bh_the} is the same stone. The hand held out for yours is the great-great-grandchild of the hand that asked the first time. The words have been changed a little, since a scholar has found that the old ones had a hole in them. They would so like you to say it again, so that the young, who were not there, may hear it. You remember what you swore last time, and to whom, and that all of them are dead.

choices.text: Say it again

effects.log: You lay your palm on it again. The groove is about the shape of your hand by now. The young relax. Somewhere under the words, you can hear yourself counting how many of these you have left in you.

choices.text: Ask what happened to the hole

ok.log: The scholar is delighted to explain. You listen with deep attention, and at the end you point out the new one. It is a long winter for the scholar. Nobody asks you to touch the stone again in this generation.

fail.log: There is no new hole. It is a very good scholar. You have the cold feeling of having been read, for the first time in a hundred years.

events.text: After a century, you know the rhythm of the people they send. They come at about twenty, they are very good, and they get older, and at about fifty they start bringing you soup. The one {npc} has just sent is the granddaughter of the last one, or the grandson, and has the same way of straightening your papers. You have been fond of that family for some time. You wonder if they know how many of them you have buried.

choices.text: Ask how the old one is keeping

effects.log: There is a very small silence. "The old one is well," says your spy, "and sends regards." So they do know. You send back a jar of the pickles the old woman liked, and go on with your papers.

choices.text: Leave out something true, for them to find

effects.log: You leave one true thing on the desk, about {npc}. In a house this old the spies are the only people who really listen to you. It would be a shame to waste them.

events.text: They have tried this one on you before: the chest under the floor, the helpful witness. {npc} does not know that, since it was before {his} time and the people who remember are all you. It is even the same floorboard. You stand in your rooms watching {him} find the chest, with exactly the same little start of surprise that {his} great-uncle used, and you find you are nearly overcome with something like nostalgia.

choices.text: Show them the other chest, from last time

effects.log: You lift the next board along. There it is, dated, with a great-uncle's seal on it, where you left it sixty years ago for just this morning. {npc} sits down. The whole room is very careful not to laugh.

mem.note: kept the last one for sixty years

choices.text: Take the blame, as an old fool might

effects.log: You sigh and pay up. It is not very much, at this point in your life. They have taken a little of your name and told you precisely who is running things now.

events.text: There is an old ledger in the house of {bh_the}, kept in the third elder's hand, of attempts to be rid of you. It is the only history of the family that has never been falsified. You have read it, naturally. It has reached a second volume. This year's entry is very likely the man on the roof, who has been up there since Tuesday in a thin coat, and who is getting a cold. It has started to rain.

choices.text: Send up a hot drink and a blanket

effects.log: You send them up with the houseboy, who is told to say nothing. The roof is empty by morning, and the blanket is folded on the sill. It goes into the second volume, you hear, as "postponed."

choices.text: Go up there and have the conversation

ok.log: You are both quite wet by the end of it. He gives you the name without being asked very hard, and you see him to the road. That name is written in your own book, which is shorter and more accurate.

fail.log: He is much better than he looked in that coat. You get back in through the window with a hole in you. You will have to make your own entry in the ledger.

events.text: It has become a kind of rite in {bh_the}. Every thirty years or so, a young and brilliant senior reads the records, sees how long you have been here and how much you know, and decides to do something for the good of the sect. This year's has poisoned your inkstone, which is an elegant idea, and which you first saw done before their teacher's teacher was born. You do so hate to discourage them.

choices.text: Send it back, with marks on their last essay

effects.log: You send the inkstone back, with some corrections to the poison and a good mark for effort. They come to see you within the week, white in the face. They are going to be very good, if they live.

choices.text: Report it to the seat, this time

effects.log: You report it. The young one is sent down the mountain. It is the right thing, and you are tired, and you remember that you once liked the ones who tried.

events.text: The new law master of {bh_the} has spent two years on your file, and {npc} has been helping. There are four hundred pages. They bring it to the council and lay it on the table with some ceremony: a century of small irregularities, every one of them true. You did all of that. You had rather hoped somebody would notice one day. It is almost a compliment.

choices.text: Ask to add the ones they missed

ok.log: You supply eleven more, with dates, and you show that each one saved the sect something it is still living on. The council reads it into the night. By morning it is less an indictment than a history.

fail.log: They are all quite aware of what it saved. They would like you to be aware of it too, in a smaller office.

choices.text: Pay the fines, every one

effects.log: It takes a good while to add up. You pay it in full and on time, which has not happened to the sect treasurer in living memory. Nobody can think of anything else to say.

events.text: A person who lives this long in {bh_the} gets to be something of a curiosity. Young assassins of the upper halls have started to treat you as a kind of graduation. You have found four of them this decade. They are very respectful about it. The one in your wardrobe tonight has plainly read about the last four, and has tried to allow for them, and is breathing almost perfectly.

choices.text: Knock on the wardrobe, and ask if they would like tea

effects.log: A long pause, and then the door opens. They would like tea. You give them some notes on their breathing. You do not know why you do this now. It could be that nobody else alive has ever got this far.

choices.text: Settle it, here and now

ok.log: It does not take long. You pay for the wardrobe. Word goes down to the upper halls that the graduation is not yet to be recommended.

fail.log: They have really allowed for you, this time. You win it. It is a near thing, and you sit up for a long while afterward.

events.text: They have accused you of treason on the high terrace of {bh_the} again. You have been accused of it under five masters of this Cult, and you have by now been guilty of it twice. {npc} presents the evidence with great flair. It is rather good, and it is about the wrong treason. In all fairness you should probably say something, and you find yourself quite curious to see where {he} is going with this.

choices.text: Let {him} finish, and applaud

effects.log: You applaud. You offer some suggestions about the third witness. The terrace is delighted, and nothing further is heard of the matter. {npc} will want to be very careful for some time.

choices.text: Confess to the other one

effects.log: You tell them about the other one, since everyone involved is dead. It is a very good story. The master laughs until the wine spills. It costs you some standing, and it buys you another decade.

events.text: It has been a very long time since you took the seat of {bh_the}. {bh_oldhead} is a name that the young have to look up. And yet every year, on the same night, someone still leaves a single white flower on the step of the old head's tablet, and nobody ever sees who. {npc} would like you to know that {he} has no idea. You have taken to getting up early that morning to see it.

choices.text: Leave it where it is

effects.log: You leave it. Some years you stand there for a time. Nobody in this house has ever told you that you have paid enough, and you have stopped waiting to hear it.

choices.text: Add a second flower

effects.log: You put your own beside it. The next year, there are two again, and the one that is not yours has been moved a little further from yours. It is the longest conversation you have ever had with this family.

events.text: A young scholar of {bh_the} is writing the family's history, and {npc} has made sure that you have been shown the chapter about you. It is scrupulously fair. It gives your deeds and your dates. It runs to four lines, and the word it uses for you is the word for a long hard winter: something the house came through. You have ruled here longer than anyone in its whole history.

choices.text: Sign the chapter as it stands

effects.log: You sign it. The scholar is very surprised. Four lines is about what you would have written yourself, on the morning after, a very long time ago.

choices.text: Have it rewritten

effects.log: It is rewritten, at some length, in beautiful language. Everyone can tell. The scholar's first draft is being copied by hand in the family wing, and you know that too.

events.text: At {bh_the} they now teach your coup as a lesson: a case study for the third-year students, with diagrams. {npc} teaches it. You went to sit at the back of the class once, and nobody dared to stop you. They have most of it right. They have made you cleverer than you were, and much less frightened, and {bh_oldhead} comes out of it rather well. The diagrams are good.

choices.text: Say nothing, and stay to the end

effects.log: You stay to the end, and you hand in the exercise along with the rest. You get a middling mark. {npc} has not slept since.

choices.text: Tell them what it was really like

effects.log: You stand up at the back and you tell them about the smell of the hall, and your hands. It is very quiet. Several of them change their essays. {npc} takes the diagrams down that night.

events.text: Everyone in {bh_the} who hated you for the seat is dead. It took a long time, and you did not kill them all. Their children are dead too. {npc}, who brings your tea, has told you quite honestly that {he} does not hate you at all: {he} only wants the chair, as anyone would. It ought to be restful. You find you rather miss {bh_oldhead}, who at least knew exactly what you had done.

choices.text: Drink the tea

effects.log: You drink the tea, and you look at {npc} across the cup. It is only tea, today. Strength is law. It has never in all these years been a very good conversationalist.

choices.text: Give {him} a harder post, and see how long {he} lasts

effects.log: You give {him} the southern mines. {He} thanks you. You have taken to doing this every few decades. It keeps the arithmetic honest, and it passes the time.

events.text: You were born to {bh_the} a very long time ago, and you are by now the oldest person with its name. The guest at the lower table is the great-grandchild of the guest who was at the lower table when you were young, and {npc} is telling them where they may not stand. You know how this goes. You know how it went four hundred years ago, too: you have read the first page of the register.

choices.text: Stand there yourself, and ask them over

effects.log: You stand on the forbidden stone and you ask the guest to bring a stool. At your age you are entitled to be strange. {npc} goes off to complain to someone, and finds that nobody left outranks you.

choices.text: Say nothing, and go on being the house

effects.log: You go on, because someone must. The name goes on. You find that you have stopped being sure whether you are keeping it or it is keeping you.

events.text: {npc} is the last of those who ever took your side at {bh_the}, and {he} is very old now, in the way that people get while you are not looking. {He} has had {him}self carried to your door, against all advice. "They are going to try again in the spring," {he} says. "I thought you should know. I do not think I will be here for the summer. It has been very interesting. Do try to remember my name."

choices.text: Sit with {him} until dark

effects.log: You sit with {him} until it is dark, and you talk about people only the two of you remember. You have been told a good many secrets in this house, and that was the last one you will ever be told for love.

mem.note: sat with me until dark

choices.text: Be ready by spring

effects.log: You thank {him} and you have {him} carried home, gently. You are ready by spring. {He} would have approved of that, and you do remember the name.

events.text: It turns out that {npc} has been reporting on you to {bh_the} for forty years. You found out because {he} told you, last night, over the stones, in the middle of a game. {He} is old and {he} has outlived anyone who would pay {him}, and {he} would like to know whether you knew. You did not know. It has been a long while since anyone has been able to surprise you. You find that you are smiling.

choices.text: Tell {him} it is {his} move

effects.log: You look at the board for some time. "It is your move," you say. {He} plays. {He} comes back next week, and neither of you ever mentions it again, and that is friendship, here.

choices.text: Ask what {he} told them

effects.log: You go through it together, year by year, with a jug. {He} has an excellent memory. By morning you know exactly what they think of you, and you owe {him} a good many things you cannot name.

events.text: They have been looking at you in {bh_the} differently since the questioning. They know now what you are, and how long you hid it. And it is one thing to fear a strong guest, but it is quite another to discover that the modest retainer you have been sending to mend the roof has been sitting at your table for years and watching you with those eyes. Everything you ever overheard, they are going back through it now. All of it. {bh_head} no longer sends for you alone.

choices.text: Say that you were only careful, and let them think about that

effects.log: You say it to anyone who asks. Nobody asks twice. You have never been treated with so much courtesy, or sat with your back to so few doors. Whatever they have planned, it has got a good deal worse.

choices.text: Go to the head of the house, and offer the truth

ok.log: You tell the head of the house more or less everything. They do not thank you. But they look at you for a long while, and then they ask you what you saw that they should have seen. It does not undo it. It does make you useful, and that is the one thing they cannot afford to waste.

fail.log: They hear you to the end. "And now you are being honest," they say, in a voice like a closing door. "I see. Thank you."

events.text: The cook has stopped speaking to you. That is what finally gets to you. The whole of {bh_the} has gone quiet around you since they saw through the seal, as you always knew it might, and you were ready for the elders. You were not ready for the old woman in the kitchen who has been putting an extra ladle in your bowl for years because she thought that you were poor. She puts the bowl down on the table now, and goes back to her fire.

choices.text: Tell her why you did it

effects.log: She goes on stirring for a very long time. "I had a boy," she says, "who thought he was clever too." You have your extra ladle the next day. It is not because she has forgiven you.

choices.text: Eat, and leave the silver on the table

effects.log: You leave it. She leaves it there as well. It is still on the table at the end of the month, and at the end of the next. You understand. You stop leaving it, and you eat your dinner in your rooms.

events.text: A promotion list has gone up on the wall of the guest wing of {bh_the}. You are not on it. Neither, for the sixth year, is your name mentioned in the margin where they write the ones who may come along later. A boy you taught to hold a sword is on it. "It is only that you have rather levelled off," says the master of retainers, kindly, patting your arm. He can feel nothing through your sleeve. You could stop his heart from here.

choices.text: Congratulate the boy

effects.log: You buy the boy a drink. He tells you what they are saying in the upper hall, because he thinks nothing of telling you things. He tells you a good deal. That is what the sleeve is for.

choices.text: Let the master of retainers feel what he is patting

effects.log: He takes his hand away very slowly. Nobody in the yard knows why the old man has sat down on the ground. By evening they all do, and your name goes up on the wall, and every elder of the blood has started counting back the years you have been in the house.

events.text: The heir of {bh_the} has had a bad day, and has chosen you to have it on. "You," says {bh_heir}, in front of the whole guard, "have been here for how long? And you are still what you are? Some people are simply furniture." There is laughter. They are about to lay out the family's entire plan for the river war in front of you, because it is the same thing as doing it in front of a chair.

choices.text: Hold the lamp a little higher

effects.log: You hold it higher. You hear about the fords, and the numbers, and the cousin who will not be coming back from the left flank. You are a very good chair. When the time comes, you will know exactly where each leg of this table stands.

choices.text: Set the lamp down, and let the seal go

effects.log: The lamp does not flicker. Everything else does. {bh_heir} stops talking and the guard stop breathing, and you look across the map at them for as long as you like. They will never again say anything in front of you, and they will never again forget you are there.

events.text: A match has been announced in {bh_the}, the kind that goes to people worth binding. It goes to the guest in the next room, who is half what you are, and whose realm can be felt across a yard. Nobody has thought of you. The matchmaker went right by your door, with her scrolls, the way one walks past a bucket. She has actually hung her wet umbrella on your door handle while she knocks next door.

choices.text: Dry her umbrella for her

effects.log: You dry it. She thanks you and calls you by the wrong name. Nobody will ever try to tie you to anything in this house. It is quite lonely, and it is quite safe, and it is exactly what you paid for.

choices.text: Hand it to her, and let her feel the handle

effects.log: She looks at the umbrella, and at you, and sits down quite suddenly on her scrolls. By morning there are nine of them at your door. They are all very flattering, and every one of them has been sent by someone who is very frightened.
